paper.title: 12th International Olympiad on Astronomy and Astrophysics — Observational Competition and Mountain Team Competition
paper.caveat: The archive includes separate suggested KOR corrections. O4 changes the accepted constellation; O5 proposes 1.7° while the final night key prints 1.8°. Both versions and their original scoring are retained. The Mountain task has no supplied key.

transcription.verifiedBy: mechanical:single-pass-gates (single-pass source transcription; automated schema, math and crop-evidence checks; no separate model checker, prompt v2)
transcription.notes: Astra single-pass personal visual reading of the full matched source pack. Preserve all seven independent original problems and IDs. Recover six official keys and scoring; distinguish suggested KOR correction documents from final day/night keys without silently adopting either discrepancy. No separate checker. Day and night instructions are scoped to their own problems. All original question diagrams retained. All 20 prepared pages personally read. The three KOR DOCX members retain real ZIP/member provenance. Original uncorrected ZIP DOCX keys were text-compared to the final PDFs, not separately claimed as visually read. The separately archived team question supplies no key. All nine final no-snap crops personally viewed after upload, including full answer chart and every question photograph. ZIP helper exported all five correction pages; personally compared those against the scratch exports before freeze.

problems.title: O1
problems.statement:
**Day — Instructions**

1. This part of the contest consists of 4 problems, is 1 hour long and is worth a total of 100 points.

2. Only blue pen should be used to fill in the answer boxes, draw and mark on the star chart.

3. You are not allowed to leave your working desk without permission. If you need any assistance (malfunctioning calculator, need to visit a restroom, etc.), please put up your hand to signal the supervisor.

4. The beginning and end of the competition will be indicated by a long sound signal.

5. Wait at your table until your envelope is collected. Once all envelopes are collected, your student guide will escort you out of the competition area.

Figure 1 is a whole sky star chart of Yanqing, Beijing at 20:30 tonight (UTC+8) with the limit magnitude = $5^{\mathrm{m}}$ (m = magnitude). Four stars (about $1^{\mathrm{m}}$ - $3^{\mathrm{m}}$) and one planet (brighter than $2^{\mathrm{m}}$) are missing in this chart. In the chart, the distance from the centre is in proportion to zenith distance

figures.caption: Figure 1
figures.alt: Circular whole-sky star chart: a large circle filled with black dots of different sizes (stars down to the limiting magnitude), with no coordinate grid, no constellation lines, no labels and no orientation marks.

parts.statement: Draw a cross (X) on the location of each missing star and mark “T” on the chart, and draw a cross (X) on the location of the missing planet and mark “P” on the chart.
Please mark the orientation of the star chart with “N” “E” “S” “W” at the edge of the star chart.
On the chart, the celestial equator passes through many constellations. Please write down the name of any five of these constellations (IAU codes).
Using the star chart, estimate the altitude of Aldebaran (α Tau), to the nearest degree.

sections.title: (1) (20 points)
sections.statement:
See figure 1. P = Mars. Stars = α Aql, α Cep, ε Cas, α Ari. (anticlockwise)

4 points for each. Inside the small circle = 4 points. Between the small and big circle = 2 points.

sections.title: (2) (5 points)
sections.statement:
See figure 1.

1 point for each. 5 points for all. Between the curve = 1 point.

sections.title: (3) (10 points)
sections.statement:
From west to east: Ophiuchus (Oph), Serpens (Ser), Aquila (Aql), Aquarius (Aqr), Pisces (Psc), Cetus (Cet), Taurus (Tau), Eridanus (Eri), Orion (Ori).

2 point for each. 10 points for 5 or more.

sections.title: (4) (5 points)
sections.statement:
18.33°.

5 points for 16° ~ 21°, 3 points for 13° ~ 15° and 22° ~ 24°, 1 point for 10° ~ 12° and 25° ~ 27°.

figures.alt: Official answer chart with P, the four missing-star target circles, and N, E, S, W orientation marks and scoring curves.

Figure 2 is a star chart of a recent opposition of Jupiter. The grid in the figure is the ecliptic coordinates. Please estimate the date of this opposition, to the nearest day.

figures.caption: Figure 2
figures.alt: Star chart with an ecliptic coordinate grid: slightly tilted lines of ecliptic latitude 10°, 0° (thick line, the ecliptic) and −10°, and lines of ecliptic longitude labelled 300°, 290°, 280° and 270°. Dotted lines mark constellation boundaries. The label “Sgr” is at upper left; the stars of Sagittarius are joined by constellation lines and labelled with Greek letters (μ, λ, δ, γ, ε, σ, φ, τ, ζ, π, ο, ω, ρ, χ and others). A large black dot labelled “Jupiter” lies on the ecliptic just east of the 290° longitude line.

solution.statement:
July 7.

20 points for July 5 ~ July 9, 12 points for July 2 ~ July 4 and July 10 ~ July 12, 6 points for June 29 ~ July 1 and July 13 ~ July 15.

Figure 3 is a star chart of a part of the sky on March 21, 2018. The longitude and latitude of the observation site is 120°E, 40°N (UTC+8). The grid in the figure is an equatorial grid. The thicker vertical line in the centre is the meridian. Estimate the mean solar time to an accuracy of better than 0.5h.

figures.caption: Figure 3
figures.alt: Star chart of part of the sky with an equatorial grid: declination circles labelled 30°, 0° and −30°, and hour circles labelled 14h, 12h, 10h and 8h. A thick vertical line through the centre is the meridian, marked N at the top and S at the bottom. Stars are drawn as black dots joined by constellation lines, without constellation names. A grey band along the bottom of the chart shows the region below the horizon.

problems.title: O5
problems.statement:
**Night — Instructions**

1. This part of the competition consists of 2 problems (O5 and O6), and is worth a total of 50 points.

2. You have 10 minutes to complete these problems.

3. Stop working once the timer expires.

4. At the end of the examination, hand over the test envelope to the supervisor at the station.

5. You will use a telescope to observe five red LED screens at a distance. The telescope is equipped with one eyepiece, but no finderscope. Some of these screens display the names of planets, some show Messier numbers, and some show equatorial coordinates.

**The eyepiece’s field of view is 45°.** Please estimate the field of view (with an accuracy of 0.1°) of the telescope when observing.

sections.title: Official night solution
sections.statement:
$$
F\tan(\mathrm{FOV}/2)=f\tan(45^\circ/2)
$$

$F=700\,\mathrm{mm},\ f=26\,\mathrm{mm}$

$$
\mathrm{FOV}/2=\operatorname{Arctan}(0.414f/F)=0.881^\circ
$$

$$
\mathrm{FOV}=2\times0.881^\circ=1.76^\circ\approx1.8^\circ
$$

10 points for 1.6° ~ 1.9°, 5 points for 1.3° ~ 1.5° and 2.0° ~ 2.2°.

sections.title: Suggestion by KOR — Night-Cloudy correction
sections.statement:
2.13°

$$
F\tan(\mathrm{FOV})=f\tan45^\circ
$$

$F=700\,\mathrm{mm},\ f=26\,\mathrm{mm}$

$$
\mathrm{FOV}=\operatorname{Arctan}(f/F)=2.13^\circ\approx2.1^\circ
$$

10 points for 2.0° ~ 2.2°, 5 points for 1.6° ~ 1.9° and 2.3° ~ 2.5°.

In order to get the correct FOV, we have to use (45/2)° instead of 45°

Therefore, correct answer should be 1.7° instead of 2.13°

sections.title: Suggestion by KOR — Readme
sections.statement:
2. Night (Cloudy) – O5

In order to get the correct FOV, we have to use (45/2)° not just 45°

Therefore, correct answer should be 1.7° instead of 2.13°

problems.title: Mountain
problems.statement:
**Instruction**

First and foremost, safety should be your main concern ！

You can see mountains around the hotel, and in the picture below, the highest peak is marked with an arrow. Estimate the height of this peak relative to the ground of the hotel. You can use everything you can get or make, except climbing up! The team which gives a number closest to the actual answer will win the ‘game’.

Give this page to the organizers or volunteers before 23:59, November 8th.
